screens.title: Files, Directories, and Permissions
screens.narratorSegment: Linux is built as a multi-user system, and managing who can access files is one of the first skills you need on a Raspberry Pi. In this lesson you will learn what owner and group mean, how read, write and execute bits control behavior, how to read the compact output of the list command that shows permissions, and how to change settings safely with chmod and chown. You will also learn when to use sudo and why caution matters. These controls protect your system, keep your work private, and prevent accidental deletions or insecure scripts from running. For example, a notes file might be readable only by you, while a shared directory might let others list files but not modify them. As you study, pay attention to patterns you can reuse: permission triplets for owner, group, and others; numeric permission sums; and symbolic adjustments like adding execute to a script. By the end of this chapter you will be able to read permission strings, set permissions for a file and a directory to match practical needs, and follow a safe checklist before using sudo. Think about how you would protect a configuration file and what permissions you would grant to a shared folder. That choice is the core of secure file management on the Pi.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Files, Directories, and Permissions
Files, Directories, and Permissions
Control who can read, write, or run each file on your Pi.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Owner & Group

Every file has an owner and a group that determine default access. Think of ownership as who controls a file and group as a team membership.

Permission Bits

Three sets of permissions for owner, group, and others: read, write, execute. They behave slightly differently for directories.

Commands

Use ls -l to inspect, chmod to change permissions, and chown to change ownership. sudo is required for administrative changes.

In this lesson
Read permissions, set permissions, and use sudo with care. Hands-on examples included.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will understand how Linux represents file permissions, be able to read the compact output of ls -l, change permissions with both symbolic and numeric chmod forms, and manage file ownership safely with chown and sudo. First, you will learn the conceptual model: every file has an owner, a group, and three permission sets controlling read, write, and execute for those roles. Second, you will practice reading ls -l examples and translating the string -rw-r--r-- into who can do what. Third, you'll use symbolic chmod commands like add execute for the owner, remove write for group and others, and the numeric form such as chmod 755 to set typical script permissions. Finally, you'll learn when and why sudo is required to change ownership and why it must be used carefully. These objectives matter because they directly affect the security and functionality of your Pi: too-permissive files let others change or run code, while too-restrictive settings can break scripts. Each objective includes a small practical exercise so you not only understand the theory but can verify it on your own Pi.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on concrete practice and safety. You will apply permission knowledge to two small tasks: create a private file accessible only to the owner, and create a shared directory with controlled access for group members. Each task makes the abstract bits practical: setting a file to owner read-write prevents others from viewing secrets, while giving a directory execute but not write to some users lets them enter and list but not create files. You'll also learn safe sudo habits: when changing ownership with chown, you usually need sudo. Before running any sudo command, check which file you are targeting and why you need root privileges. Mistakes with sudo can change system files or expose sensitive data. The practice exercises ask you to verify results with ls -la and to reason about whether the permissions match the intended access. These verification steps are essential to build confidence and avoid common errors like forgetting the execute bit on a script or making a file world-writable by accident. The habit of testing with ls after every change is the simplest safety net.

screens.title: Linux multi-user model and ownership
screens.narratorSegment: Linux treats a Raspberry Pi as a shared environment where many accounts may exist. Every file and directory records two key identity fields: the owner and the group. The owner is the user who controls the file by default and usually created it. The group is a named collection of users that can be used to grant the same permissions to a team. Together with three sets of permission bits, owner and group form the complete access model. For example, if a file is owned by user alex and group staff, alex has the owner permissions, any user in staff has the group permissions, and everyone else falls into the others category. This model matters because it lets you apply different rules for personal files versus team-shared files without needing separate copies. A common misconception is thinking group and others are identical — they are different buckets. Another mistake is relying only on default group settings; explicitly checking and adjusting group membership is often necessary to make sharing work. Concrete example: create a file as alex and add other users to the file's group to let them read the file without granting global access. Quick takeaway: ownership decides whose permission bits apply, group provides team-level access, and others is the rest of the system users.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Ownership
Owner, Group, Others
Definition and how they map to permission sets.
Owner
User who created or was assigned the file; owner permissions apply to them.
Group
Named team that can be given shared access using the group permission bits.
Others
All other users on the system who are neither the owner nor in the file's group.
Example
If alex:staff owns notes.txt and perms are -rw-r-----, alex can read/write, staff can read, others have no access. Add a user to staff to grant them team read access without making the file public.
Supporting Details
  • Ownership fields are visible in ls -l output as two columns: owner and group names.
  • Changing group membership is often necessary when sharing files within a team.
  • chown changes owner and optionally group; chgrp changes group only.
Analogy
Owner is the file's keyholder, group is a shared key for a team, others are people outside the team.
Common mistake
Assuming everyone in group has the same shell or environment; group controls only file access, not user settings.

screens.title: Reading ls -l output
screens.narratorSegment: The ls -l command gives a concise, information-dense view of files and directories. A typical line looks like: dash rw dash r dash r dash, then a number, owner, group, size, timestamp, and name. The first character tells you the file type: a dash is a regular file, and a d is a directory. The next nine characters are three groups of three that represent owner, group, and others. Each group uses r for read, w for write, and x for execute; a dash means that permission is not granted. For example, -rw-r--r-- means the owner can read and write, group can read, and others can read. The number after the permissions is the link count, then the owner and group names, then the size and last modification time. A concrete example is -rw-r--r-- 1 alex alex 1234 Jun 10 09:15 notes. txt which tells you alex owns it, alex's group is set as group, file size is 1234 bytes, and the name is notes. txt. A common misconception is treating the permission string as symmetric for files and directories; remember directory execute means ability to enter the directory. Closing question: given a sample ls -l line, can you identify who can create files inside a directory and who can only list entries?

keyIdea.text: ls -l packs type, permissions, link count, owner, group, size, time, and name. Learn the order and what each field signals for access control.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Reading ls -l
Parse an ls -l line
Break the string into parts and interpret permissions.
-rw-r--r-- 1 alex alex 1234 Jun 10 09:15 notes.txt
• First char: file type (dash = file, d = directory).
• Next 9 chars: permissions in three triplets: owner, group, others.
• Numbers and names: link count, owner, group, size, timestamp, name.
Key Takeaway

Reading ls -l is the fastest way to verify who can do what with a file. Use it after each change.

Walkthrough: Interpret example
Owner: alex — owner bits are rw- so alex can read and write but not execute. Group: alex — group bits are r-- so group members can read only. Others: r-- so anyone can read. This suggests a text file intended to be readable by all but only editable by alex.
Misconception
Execute on a directory is not running code. It lets you change into the directory and traverse it. Listing is controlled by read.
Check
If a directory shows drwxr-xr-x, who can create files inside it? Only the owner, because group and others lack write permission.

screens.title: Read, Write, Execute: File vs Directory
screens.narratorSegment: Read, write, and execute permissions apply to both files and directories, but their practical effects differ and that's critical to understand. For files, read allows viewing the file content, write allows modifying the file, and execute allows running the file as a program or script. For directories, read lets you list filenames inside, write lets you create, remove, or rename entries, and execute grants the ability to enter the directory and traverse it to access nested entries. A common error is setting a directory readable but not executable: you can see filenames but cannot cd into or access files within. Concrete example: if a shared folder has permissions r-x for the group, group members can enter and list contents if read is set, but cannot create new files because write is disabled. Conversely, if write is enabled but execute is not, members cannot actually enter to create files. Remember that scripts need the execute bit to be run directly; a script with rw- for the owner will not run until you add x. Closing question: when giving others access to a folder for collaboration, which bits do you typically set and why?

Conversely, if write is enabled but execute is not, members cannot actually enter to create files. Remember that scripts need the execute bit to be run directly; a script with rw- for the owner will not run until you add x. Closing question: when giving others access to a folder for collaboration, which bits do you typically set and why?

keyIdea.title: Same letters, different actions
keyIdea.text: r, w, x mean different things on directories: read = list, write = create/delete, execute = enter/traverse. Set them together thoughtfully for desired behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Permissions: File vs Directory
Permissions on files
  • Read: open and view file contents.
  • Write: edit or replace the file contents.
  • Execute: run the file as a program or script.
Example: chmod u+x script.py adds execute for the owner so the script can be run directly.
Permissions on directories
  • Read: list filenames in the directory.
  • Write: create, delete, or rename files inside.
  • Execute: enter or traverse the directory with cd and access contained files if permitted.
Example: drwxr-xr-x means owner can do everything, group and others can list and enter but not create files.
Common mistake and check
If collaborators report they cannot create files, verify the directory group and owner bits include write. If they can see names but cannot access files, check execute permission is set so traversal is allowed.

screens.title: chmod — Symbolic mode
screens.narratorSegment: Symbolic mode for chmod uses human-readable letter codes to adjust permissions without calculating numbers. The basic parts are who: u for user (owner), g for group, o for others, and a for all; an operator: plus to add, minus to remove, equals to set exactly; and permission letters: r, w, x. For example, chmod u+x script dot P Y file adds execute for the owner so the owner can run the script. chmod go-w notes. txt removes write from group and others so only the owner can edit. Using a combination like chmod a+r document. txt gives read permission to all. Symbolic mode is ideal when you want to make small changes without affecting other bits. A typical process is: 1) inspect current permissions with ls -l, 2) plan the minimal change you need, 3) run chmod with the symbolic expression, and 4) verify with ls -l again. A common misconception is assuming plus or minus will only target a single bit—if you use equals you overwrite the full set for that who field. For example chmod g=rw will set group to read and write only, removing execute if it existed. Final reflection: prefer symbolic mode for targeted edits and always verify after change.

keyIdea.title: Symbolic edits
keyIdea.text: Symbolic chmod is clear and safe for incremental permission changes: pick who, operator, and permission letters, then verify the result.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › chmod Symbolic
Symbolic syntax
who (u/g/o/a), operator (+/-/=), permissions (r/w/x)
Examples
chmod u+x script.py — add execute for owner.
chmod go-w notes.txt — remove write for group and others.
chmod a+r document.txt — add read for everyone.
Process
1. Inspect with ls -l. 2. Decide minimal change. 3. Run chmod symbolic. 4. Verify with ls -l.
Misconception
Using equals sets the full set for that who field and can remove permissions you didn't intend to change. Use plus or minus to adjust bits safely.
Try this

Try adding execute to a script with chmod u+x and confirm you can run it. If it still fails, check the file's shebang or interpreter and whether you invoked it correctly.

screens.title: chmod — Numeric mode
screens.narratorSegment: Numeric mode expresses permissions as three digits, one for owner, group, and others. Each permission is a value you sum: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1. For example, 7 is 4+2+1 meaning read, write, execute. 5 is 4+1 meaning read and execute. A common pattern is chmod 755 script dot P Y file which gives the owner full rights and group and others read and execute so they can run but not edit the file. Another common numeric permission is 644 for text files where owner can read and write (6 = 4+2) and group and others can only read (4). Numeric mode is compact and useful when you want to set all three categories at once. A common error is forgetting to include the execute bit for scripts, making them non-runnable even though they contain valid code. When using numeric mode, write down the intended bits: owner X, group Y, others Z, then convert to numbers. Example mapping: owner rwx = 7, group r-x = 5, others r-- = 4 so 754. Closing reflection: numeric mode is fast and precise but double-check the digits to avoid unintended access.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › chmod Numeric
Permission values
Read = 4, Write = 2, Execute = 1. Sum them for each category: owner, group, others.
Owner Group Others 7 5 5 → chmod 755 script.py
6 4 4 → chmod 644 file.txt (owner rw, group r, others r)
Key Takeaway

Numeric mode is concise for one-step permission settings. Always verify the resulting bits after running the command.

Common mistakes
  • Omitting execute for scripts when you expect to run them directly.
  • Using 777 which makes files world-writable and is usually unsafe.
  • Applying numeric chmod recursively without understanding its impact on directories versus files.
Practice
Convert intended bits to digits before running chmod, then confirm with ls -l.

screens.title: Symbolic vs Numeric chmod
screens.narratorSegment: Both symbolic and numeric modes for chmod are valid and each has strengths. Symbolic mode is explicit about whom you change and which bits you add or remove, making it safer for incremental edits. Numeric mode is compact and convenient when you want to set all three categories at once. For example, to make a script executable for the owner only, symbolic chmod u+x is clear and low-risk. To set a standard executable permission for a project directory you might use chmod 755. A common confusion arises when people try to mix the two mentally and forget that equals in symbolic mode overwrites bits. Another practical point: when scripting or provisioning multiple files, numeric mode is simpler to express in automation scripts, but ensure the digits match your intent for directories and files. Example mapping table: chmod u+x ↔ owner gains 1, whereas chmod 700 sets owner to rwx and others to nothing; these are not equivalent operations. Misconception check: chmod 755 does not grant write to group or others, only to owner. Closing question: which mode would you choose to remove write from group and others for a single file, and why?

keyIdea.text: Use symbolic mode for targeted edits and numeric mode for bulk, consistent settings. Always verify the final permission string with ls -l.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Symbolic vs Numeric
Symbolic
Good for incremental, human-readable changes. Example: chmod u+x script.py
Operator-based: who (+/-/=) + perms. Safer for single edits.
Watch out: equals overwrites existing bits.
Numeric
Good for concise, one-line settings of all categories. Example: chmod 755 script.py
Three digits: owner, group, others — each is sum of 4,2,1.
Watch out: it's easy to mistype a digit and grant too much access.
Quick decision guide
If you want to modify one bit use symbolic. If you want to set a standard set across many files or in automation, numeric is faster. Always verify with ls -l.

screens.title: chown and chgrp — changing ownership
screens.narratorSegment: chown changes the owner and optionally the group of a file, and chgrp changes only the group. Ownership changes often require sudo because only root can give files to other users or alter system-owned files. The typical usage is sudo chown root:root sensitive_file. txt which sets both owner and group to root. Another pattern is chown alex:staff file. txt to change owner to alex and group to staff. A practical example: when moving configuration files into system directories, you may need to chown them to root, but doing so accidentally on files in your home directory can prevent your account from editing them. A common mistake is using chown on many files recursively without checking which files should remain owned by other users. Always inspect which files will be affected and prefer to change ownership only when necessary. After changing ownership, verify with ls -l that the owner and group columns reflect the new values. Closing question: before you run sudo chown on a directory tree, what verification step should you perform to avoid breaking access for other users? chown and chgrp — changing ownership means use chown to set owner and group. most chown operations need sudo, so double-check targets and scope before running recursive ownership changes.. In practical terms, how to transfer file ownership and group membership safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: chown changes the owner and optionally the group of a file, and chgrp changes only the group. chown basics
Change owner and group with chown. Often requires sudo for non-user files.
sudo chown root:root sensitive_file.txt
chown alex:staff project.txt
Safety and checks
  • Use ls -l to confirm current owners before changing them.
  • Avoid recursive chown unless you know exactly which files should change.
  • Prefer changing group membership or permissions first rather than changing ownership widely.
Example scenario
You need to move a service file into a system directory. Use sudo chown root:root after copying, then verify ownership so the service runs with correct privileges. If you accidentally chown files in your home to root, you'll lose normal write access without sudo to revert changes.

screens.title: Using sudo safely
screens.narratorSegment: sudo grants elevated privileges so a permitted user can run a single command as the superuser. It's necessary for actions like changing ownership of system files, installing software, or altering global configuration. Because root can change anything, including removing system files or exposing data, use sudo only when you understand the command and its target. A safe workflow is: 1) inspect current state with ls -l, 2) run a non-destructive read-only command if possible, 3) prepare the exact sudo command and its arguments, 4) run it and then verify the outcome with ls -l. For example, use sudo chown root:root only on files that must be owned by root; avoid running random commands chained from the internet with sudo. A common misconception is that sudo is harmless just because the command worked before—some commands have side effects that escalate when run as root. If you need repeated root tasks, prefer controlled scripts that you inspect and test on a non-critical directory. Closing reflection: treat sudo as a powerful tool that requires a short checklist before use — inspect, understand, run, and verify.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Using sudo safely
Why sudo matters
It temporarily elevates privileges to do tasks that require root permissions. Use it sparingly and deliberately.
Safe workflow
Inspect, plan, run a single command, verify with ls -l.
Avoid
Do not run unclear commands from the internet with sudo; they can do irreversible damage.
Example check
Before sudo chown -R root:root /some/path, list the contents of /some/path and ensure those files should indeed be owned by root. Consider testing on a copy first.
Pro tip

If unsure, run the command without sudo first when possible, or run with echo to preview arguments in scripts before elevating.

screens.title: Task walkthrough — secret.txt and shared directory
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the hands-on activity step by step so you can practice the concepts. First, create a file called secret. txt owned by your user. Use a text editor or the touch command. Then set its permissions so only the owner can read and write. A practical sequence is: touch secret. txt, chmod 600 secret. txt, then ls -la secret. txt should show -rw-------. That confirms group and others have no access. Next, create a directory named shared with mkdir shared. Decide the sharing rules: the owner should have full access, the group should be able to read and enter, and others should only be able to enter. One set that matches that description is owner rwx (7), group r-x (5), others --x (1). You can set this with chmod 751 shared and verify with ls -ld shared which shows permission bits for the directory. If you need group members to create files in shared, give the group write as well, and ensure users are members of that group. Remember to test behavior by attempting operations as another account or by simulating with sudo -u if available. Common pitfall: forgetting the execute bit on the directory prevents entering even if read is set. After each change confirm with ls -la to close the loop. Reflection: which commands did you run and what did ls -la show each time?

Private file: secret.txt
Steps to create and lock a file to the owner.
touch secret.txt chmod 600 secret.txt ls -la secret.txt
Expect -rw------- which means only the owner can read and write.
Check
If another user needs access, adjust group and add that user to the group rather than making the file world-readable.
Shared directory: shared
Create a directory with owner full access, group read+execute, others execute only.
mkdir shared chmod 751 shared ls -ld shared
drwxr-x--x indicates owner rwx, group r-x, others --x. Adjust to 775 if group should create files.

screens.title: Common mistakes and verification
screens.narratorSegment: Permission issues are common, and a few checks will usually reveal the cause. Start with ls -l or ls -la to inspect the permission string and ownership. If a script won't run, check that the execute bit is present; chmod u+x script_name often fixes it. If users cannot create files in a directory, verify the directory's group and owner and ensure the group has write permission and that users belong to that group. Beware of recursive chmod or chown commands: chmod -R 777 /some/path will make everything world-writable and is often catastrophic from a security standpoint. Another subtle cause is umask: the default umask influences what permissions new files receive. If newly created files appear with unexpected permissions, consider checking or adjusting umask, or explicitly chmod them after creation. When ownership is wrong, sudo chown can repair it, but double-check the target and scope before running recursive ownership changes. Concrete example: if a web script fails, you might see it owned by root and not executable by the web user; fixing owner and execute bit often resolves the issue. Closing reflection: what was the last permission-related problem you had, and which of these checks would you perform first to diagnose it?

Quick diagnostic steps

Commands applying 777 or recursive ownership changes are high risk. Pause and inspect before running them.

Linux is built as a multi-user system, and managing who can access files is one of the first skills you need on a Raspberry Pi. In this lesson you will learn what owner and group mean, how read, write and execute bits control behavior, how to read the compact output of the list command that shows permissions, and how to change settings safely with chmod and chown. You will also learn when to use sudo and why caution matters. These controls protect your system, keep your work private, and prevent accidental deletions or insecure scripts from running. For example, a notes file might be readable only by you, while a shared directory might let others list files but not modify them. As you study, pay attention to patterns you can reuse: permission triplets for owner, group, and others; numeric permission sums; and symbolic adjustments like adding execute to a script. By the end of this chapter you will be able to read permission strings, set permissions for a file and a directory to match practical needs, and follow a safe checklist before using sudo. Think about how you would protect a configuration file and what permissions you would grant to a shared folder. That choice is the core of secure file management on the Pi.

By the end of this chapter you will understand how Linux represents file permissions, be able to read the compact output of ls -l, change permissions with both symbolic and numeric chmod forms, and manage file ownership safely with chown and sudo. First, you will learn the conceptual model: every file has an owner, a group, and three permission sets controlling read, write, and execute for those roles. Second, you will practice reading ls -l examples and translating the string -rw-r--r-- into who can do what. Third, you'll use symbolic chmod commands like add execute for the owner, remove write for group and others, and the numeric form such as chmod 755 to set typical script permissions. Finally, you'll learn when and why sudo is required to change ownership and why it must be used carefully. These objectives matter because they directly affect the security and functionality of your Pi: too-permissive files let others change or run code, while too-restrictive settings can break scripts. Each objective includes a small practical exercise so you not only understand the theory but can verify it on your own Pi.

This second objectives screen focuses on concrete practice and safety. You will apply permission knowledge to two small tasks: create a private file accessible only to the owner, and create a shared directory with controlled access for group members. Each task makes the abstract bits practical: setting a file to owner read-write prevents others from viewing secrets, while giving a directory execute but not write to some users lets them enter and list but not create files. You'll also learn safe sudo habits: when changing ownership with chown, you usually need sudo. Before running any sudo command, check which file you are targeting and why you need root privileges. Mistakes with sudo can change system files or expose sensitive data. The practice exercises ask you to verify results with ls -la and to reason about whether the permissions match the intended access. These verification steps are essential to build confidence and avoid common errors like forgetting the execute bit on a script or making a file world-writable by accident. The habit of testing with ls after every change is the simplest safety net.

Linux treats a Raspberry Pi as a shared environment where many accounts may exist. Every file and directory records two key identity fields: the owner and the group. The owner is the user who controls the file by default and usually created it. The group is a named collection of users that can be used to grant the same permissions to a team. Together with three sets of permission bits, owner and group form the complete access model. For example, if a file is owned by user alex and group staff, alex has the owner permissions, any user in staff has the group permissions, and everyone else falls into the others category. This model matters because it lets you apply different rules for personal files versus team-shared files without needing separate copies. A common misconception is thinking group and others are identical — they are different buckets. Another mistake is relying only on default group settings; explicitly checking and adjusting group membership is often necessary to make sharing work. Concrete example: create a file as alex and add other users to the file's group to let them read the file without granting global access. Quick takeaway: ownership decides whose permission bits apply, group provides team-level access, and others is the rest of the system users.

The ls -l command gives a concise, information-dense view of files and directories. A typical line looks like: dash rw dash r dash r dash, then a number, owner, group, size, timestamp, and name. The first character tells you the file type: a dash is a regular file, and a d is a directory. The next nine characters are three groups of three that represent owner, group, and others. Each group uses r for read, w for write, and x for execute; a dash means that permission is not granted. For example, -rw-r--r-- means the owner can read and write, group can read, and others can read. The number after the permissions is the link count, then the owner and group names, then the size and last modification time. A concrete example is -rw-r--r-- 1 alex alex 1234 Jun 10 09:15 notes. txt which tells you alex owns it, alex's group is set as group, file size is 1234 bytes, and the name is notes. txt. A common misconception is treating the permission string as symmetric for files and directories; remember directory execute means ability to enter the directory. Closing question: given a sample ls -l line, can you identify who can create files inside a directory and who can only list entries?

Read, write, and execute permissions apply to both files and directories, but their practical effects differ and that's critical to understand. For files, read allows viewing the file content, write allows modifying the file, and execute allows running the file as a program or script. For directories, read lets you list filenames inside, write lets you create, remove, or rename entries, and execute grants the ability to enter the directory and traverse it to access nested entries. A common error is setting a directory readable but not executable: you can see filenames but cannot cd into or access files within. Concrete example: if a shared folder has permissions r-x for the group, group members can enter and list contents if read is set, but cannot create new files because write is disabled. Remember that scripts need the execute bit to be run directly; a script with rw- for the owner will not run until you add x. Closing question: when giving others access to a folder for collaboration, which bits do you typically set and why?

Symbolic mode for chmod uses human-readable letter codes to adjust permissions without calculating numbers.
